terms.meaning: The chief minister of a Muslim ruler; ran the government on the ruler's behalf.
terms.period: Delhi Sultanate and Mughal empire; also Afghan kings
terms.example: After Panipat (1761), Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh was named wazir of the Mughal empire.
terms.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II, Ch. 3–4

terms.meaning: Head of the Mughal military department; kept the records of mansabdars and paid the army.
terms.example: Najib-ud-Daula held Delhi as Mir Bakhshi after Panipat (1761).
terms.source: Standard Mughal administration (Satish Chandra, Medieval India)

terms.meaning: A paymaster and recruiting officer of the army; the chief one at court was the Mir Bakhshi.
terms.source: Standard Mughal administration (Satish Chandra, Medieval India)

terms.meaning: The officer in charge of revenue and finance; in a province, the diwan collected land revenue.
terms.example: The Company became the Diwan of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765.

terms.meaning: The right to collect land revenue in a province.
terms.period: Mughal grant to the East India Company
terms.example: Treaty of Allahabad (1765): Shah Alam II gave the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

terms.meaning: Police, criminal justice and general administration of a province — the nawab's side under the Dual Government.
Title of a Mughal provincial governor who in the 18th century became an almost independent ruler.
terms.example: Sirajuddaulah, Nawab of Bengal; Shuja-ud-Daula, Nawab of Awadh.

terms.meaning: Governor of a Mughal province (suba), in charge of political and military affairs.
terms.example: Sawai Raja Jai Singh of Amber was given the subadari of Agra in 1722 (NCERT).

terms.meaning: A province of the Mughal empire.
Military officer in charge of a district (sarkar); kept law and order.
Police chief of a town.
Judge who decided cases under Islamic law.
A Mughal officer holding a rank (mansab) that fixed his status, salary and the cavalry he had to keep.
terms.example: In Akbar's reign 29 mansabdars had a rank of 5,000 zat; by Aurangzeb's reign there were 79 (NCERT).

terms.meaning: The personal rank of a mansabdar; it fixed his status and salary.
terms.example: A noble with a zat of 5,000 ranked above one with 1,000.

terms.meaning: The number of horsemen (cavalry) a mansabdar had to maintain.
Land whose revenue was assigned to a mansabdar instead of a cash salary; the holder was a jagirdar.
A landholder who collected revenue from peasants and passed part of it to the state.
terms.example: The Permanent Settlement (1793) made the zamindars of Bengal owners of the land.

terms.meaning: A large landholder or revenue collector over a group of villages (a taluq); powerful in Awadh.
terms.source: NCERT Class 8 Ch. 3; Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 11

terms.meaning: A peasant cultivator.
Revenue settled directly with each cultivator (ryot), not through a zamindar.
terms.example: Developed by Thomas Munro.

terms.meaning: Revenue settled with the village or estate (mahal) as a whole, collected by the village headman.
terms.example: Devised by Holt Mackenzie.

terms.meaning: 25 per cent of the land revenue, claimed by the Marathas from areas outside their direct rule.
9–10 per cent of the land revenue paid to the head revenue collector — claimed by the Maratha king.
The chief minister of the Maratha king; from the 18th century the real head of the Maratha state, based at Pune.
terms.example: Balaji Baji Rao was Peshwa during the Third Battle of Panipat.

terms.meaning: Title of the Maratha king (literally 'lord of the umbrella').
A chief or military commander.
terms.example: The Maratha sardars Sindhia, Holkar, Gaikwad and Bhonsle formed a confederacy under the Peshwa.

terms.meaning: An alliance of states or chiefs who act together under a common head.
terms.example: The Maratha confederacy under the Peshwa.

terms.meaning: A band of Sikh fighters under a chief; earlier called jathas, later misls (NCERT).
The combined army of all the Sikh misls.
A collective decision ('resolution of the Guru') taken by the Sikhs meeting at Amritsar.
Sikh system of protecting cultivators in return for a tax of 20 per cent of the produce.
An assembly of Afghan tribal chiefs that takes decisions by consensus.
terms.example: A jirga at Kandahar chose Ahmad Shah Abdali as king in 1747.

terms.meaning: Afghan settlers who ruled Rohilkhand (north-west of Awadh) in the 18th century.
terms.example: Najib-ud-Daula was a Rohilla chief.

terms.meaning: Soldiers trained in European-style infantry and artillery warfare.
terms.example: Ibrahim Khan Gardi led the Maratha artillery at Panipat.

terms.meaning: A free pass that let the Company trade in Bengal without paying duties; its misuse by Company servants angered the nawabs.
A royal order or grant issued by the Mughal emperor.
terms.example: Aurangzeb issued a farman letting the Company trade duty-free in Bengal (NCERT).

terms.meaning: A trading post of a European company — a warehouse where goods were stored and officials (factors) lived; not a place where goods were made.
terms.example: The first English factory in Bengal was set up on the river Hugli in 1651 (NCERT).

terms.meaning: One of the three main British administrative units — Bengal, Madras and Bombay — each headed by a governor.
A British political agent stationed at the court of an Indian ruler to watch and control him.
British troops placed in an Indian state under the Subsidiary Alliance, paid for by its ruler.
The Company's claim that its authority was supreme over all Indian states, so it could annex any of them.
Dalhousie's rule that a dependent state whose ruler died without a natural male heir would pass ('lapse') to the Company.
terms.example: Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854).

terms.meaning: The head of the Company's government in India — of Bengal from 1773, of India from 1833.
terms.example: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal.

terms.meaning: The Crown's representative in India after 1858; the Governor-General's title as the British monarch's deputy.
terms.example: Lord Canning was the first Viceroy.

terms.meaning: A body of the British government (from 1784) that directed the Company's political affairs in India.
The governing body of the East India Company in London.
A royal licence granting a company rights, such as a trade monopoly; the Company's charter was renewed by Charter Acts every 20 years.
terms.example: The English East India Company got its charter from Queen Elizabeth I in 1600.

terms.meaning: Clive's system in Bengal (1765–72): the Company had the Diwani and power, the nawab had the Nizamat and the blame.
Emperor — the title used by the Mughal rulers.
Title of a Muslim sovereign ruler, used by the rulers of Delhi before the Mughals and by others such as Tipu.
An agent or representative of a ruler at another court.
A ruler's court or a formal public assembly held by him.
terms.example: The Delhi Durbar of 1877 proclaimed Queen Victoria Empress of India.

terms.meaning: The community of initiated Sikhs founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699.
Akbar's revenue system based on measuring land and fixing tax on each crop in cash.
Revenue farming — the right to collect revenue given to the highest bidder.
Money a defeated side is made to pay to the winner after a war.
terms.example: Tipu paid a huge indemnity after the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792).

terms.meaning: A person held by one side as a guarantee that the other side keeps a treaty.
terms.example: Two of Tipu's sons were held hostage by Cornwallis in 1792.

terms.meaning: Regent of the Mughal empire — the deputy who ran it for the emperor.
terms.example: Shah Alam II made Mahadji Sindhia Vakil-ul-Mutlaq in 1784.

terms.meaning: 'Council of twelve brothers' — the Maratha ministers who ran the government for the child Peshwa Madhavrao II.
terms.example: Led by Nana Phadnis.

terms.meaning: To formally approve a treaty so that it comes into force.
terms.example: Nana Phadnis ratified the Treaty of Salbai in 1783.

terms.meaning: A party who promises that a treaty will be kept by both sides.
terms.example: Mahadji Sindhia stood guarantor of the Treaty of Salbai.

terms.meaning: A smaller state kept between two powers to keep them apart.
terms.example: Clive kept Awadh as a buffer between Bengal and the Marathas.

terms.meaning: The Old Stone Age: people hunted and gathered, and used large chipped stone tools. No farming yet.
terms.example: Tools at Jwalapuram (Kurnool) below and above the Toba ash.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: The Middle Stone Age: very small stone tools (microliths) fixed on wooden handles or arrows.
terms.period: About 10,000 to 8,000 years ago in India
terms.example: Microlith sites in the Kurnool and Nellore areas.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: The New Stone Age: polished stone axes, farming and keeping cattle in villages.
terms.period: From about 7000 BCE in the north-west; about 3000 BCE in the Deccan
terms.example: Cattle herders who made the ash mounds of Utnur.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A very small stone tool, often only a few centimetres long, used as an arrow tip or blade.
terms.example: Microliths are found in the Kurnool caves.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A large heap of ash left when Neolithic herders burnt piles of cattle dung.
terms.example: Utnur (Mahabubnagar), Budihal and Sanganakallu (Karnataka).
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A grave marked or built with big stones. "Mega" means big, "lith" means stone.
terms.period: From about 1000 BCE in the Deccan and south India
terms.example: Yeleswaram and Nagarjunakonda in Andhra.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A megalith shaped like a table: a flat stone slab on upright stones.
terms.example: Many dolmens in Krishna and Chittoor districts.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A megalith grave made as a box of stone slabs sunk in a pit.
terms.example: Cist burials are common across the Deccan.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A coffin, in the Deccan often of baked clay, sometimes with legs.
terms.example: Sarcophagus burials are common in Chittoor and Anantapuramu.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: An official order carved on a rock or pillar for people to read.
terms.example: Ashoka's edicts at Erragudi (Kurnool).
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: Ashoka's code of good conduct: respect for elders, kindness to animals and servants, tolerance of all sects.
terms.example: Rock Edict XIII names the Andhras among peoples following dhamma.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: The oldest widely used script of India; nearly all Indian scripts, including Telugu, grew from it.
terms.example: The Bhattiprolu casket uses a southern form of Brahmi.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: Everyday spoken languages of ancient India, simpler than Sanskrit; used in most early inscriptions.
terms.period: Mauryan to Satavahana and Ikshvaku times
terms.example: Hala's Gathasaptasati is in Prakrit.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A dome-shaped Buddhist mound over relics (remains) of the Buddha or a monk.
terms.example: The Amaravati Mahachaitya.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A Buddhist prayer hall, often cut into rock, with a small stupa at one end.
terms.example: The round rock-cut chaitya at Guntupalli; the Karle chaitya in Maharashtra.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A Buddhist monastery: rooms where monks lived and studied.
terms.example: The viharas of Nagarjunakonda and Thotlakonda.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: "Great shrine": the name for the great stupa at Amaravati.
terms.example: Amaravati, the biggest stupa in AP.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A small box, often of stone or crystal, holding bits of bone or ash of the Buddha, buried inside a stupa.
terms.example: The Bhattiprolu caskets.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A story about one of the Buddha's past lives; there are about 550 of them.
terms.example: The Bhimasena Jataka mentions "Andhrapatha".
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: An early Buddhist school ("the great community") that split from the elders; strong in Andhra.
terms.example: Andhra monasteries of the Krishna valley.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: "The great vehicle": a later form of Buddhism that worships the Buddha and Bodhisattvas (helpers who delay their own release to help others).
terms.example: Acharya Nagarjuna's teachings.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: "The middle way": the Mahayana school of Acharya Nagarjuna, which avoids both extremes in thinking.
terms.example: Bhavaviveka taught it at Dhanyakataka (Amaravati).
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A lay woman follower of the Buddha (a man is an upasaka).
terms.example: Bodhisiri, the upasika of the Ikshvaku age.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A name taken from the mother, such as Gautamiputra, "son of Gautami".
terms.example: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A person who rules for a king who is too young (or away).
terms.example: Queen Naganika ruled as regent for her son.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: The Vedic horse sacrifice: a horse wandered for a year, and lands it crossed unchallenged were claimed by the king.
terms.example: Satakarni I (Naneghat inscription); the Ikshvaku Chamtamula.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A guild of craftsmen or traders; it also took deposits and paid interest, like a bank.
terms.example: The Kolika (weavers') guild of the Satavahana age.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A vassal chief who ruled his own area but accepted a bigger king as overlord.
terms.example: Maharathis and Mahabhojas under the Satavahanas.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: Satrap: a governor or ruler; used by the Shaka rulers of western India (Western Kshatrapas).
terms.example: Nahapana and Rudradaman.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: Scythians: Central Asian people who ruled parts of western India; the Shaka era (78 CE) is India's national calendar.
terms.example: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated the Shaka Nahapana.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A poem of praise for a king, carved on stone.
terms.example: Harishena's Prayaga (Allahabad) pillar prashasti of Samudragupta.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A king who keeps his throne but pays tribute (regular payment) to a stronger king.
terms.example: Hastivarman of Vengi after Samudragupta.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A royal order, usually a land gift, engraved on copper sheets tied with a ring and seal.
terms.example: Salankayana and Pallava charters (Mayidavolu plates).
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts

terms.meaning: A status the Government of India gives to a very old language with a rich, independent literature.
terms.example: Telugu and Kannada got it in 2008.
terms.source: NCERT Class 6/11/12 history; standard ancient-India texts
